experiment_name: Update-budget sweep paired evaluation: baseline (0), 100, 500, 1000 updates on held-out seeds 30000-30009

algorithm_config.seat_rotation: 4 seats x 10 seeds = 40 games per checkpoint

metrics.500_vs_1000_direction: 1000's win rate (2.5%) is nominally LOWER than 500's (7.5%) - not the improvement direction at all, and unsurprisingly the non-overlap test returns false. Not claimed as a statistically supported regression (Wilson intervals [2.58%,19.86%] for 500 and [0.44%,12.88%] for 1000 overlap substantially), but flagged explicitly rather than only reporting the negative 'not improved' result - see the round-cap correction earlier in this project's history for why this distinction matters.

result: NO-SIGNAL across the board. None of the three trained checkpoints (100/500/1000 updates) show a statistically supported improvement over baseline or over each other: all four Wilson 95% intervals overlap heavily (baseline/100/1000 identical at [0.4%,12.9%] with 1/40 wins each; 500 highest at 3/40, [2.6%,19.9%], still overlapping the others). The 100-vs-500 and 500-vs-1000 non-overlap tests both return false. Notably, 500 updates had the nominally highest win rate (7.5%) of all four checkpoints, and 1000 updates fell back to baseline's win rate (2.5%) despite having by far the lowest training loss (see 015) - consistent with the value head overfitting the fixed 37,772-position replay buffer between 500 and 1000 updates without a corresponding policy improvement, though this is a descriptive observation, not a statistically tested claim. Mean/median net worth generally rose with more updates (2962 -> 3794 -> 3598 -> 4333 mean), but net worth alone is not a win-rate proxy and bankruptcy rates stayed high (50-62.5%) throughout. All four checkpoints: 0 illegal actions, 0 crashes, asu_modules_loaded count 0. ASU benchmark not run, per task instruction.
notes: Per-seed/per-seat results (160 individual games) are in the raw stdout log's per_game arrays for each checkpoint, not duplicated here. fixed_fallbacks rose noticeably with update budget (56 -> 43 -> 81 -> 76) - not investigated further here, plausibly because a more-trained search-seat model reaches different game states where the fixed opponents' scripted logic is more likely to propose an illegal action; this is about fixed-a/b/c's behavior in reached states, not a fault of our checkpoints (fixed-a/b/c fallback counting is unrelated to whether our own model acted illegally, which never happened - illegal_actions is 0 throughout).
